articles.title: Architectural Deep-Dive: OpenVLHarness: Real World Visual Agentic Tool-Use with Multimodal Memory
articles.summary: Decoupling Perception and Compute: How Persistent Multimodal Memory Fixes Agentic Tool Bottlenecks Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous visual agents tasked with analyzing technical schematics, executing system telemetry diagnostics, and verifying physical mockups. However, in production environments, a familiar wall is encountered: inference-time scaling does not solve context rot. When agents invoke diagnostic tools, search APIs, or visual crops, the naive design pattern is to inject the raw multi-megabyte payloads directly back into the conversation context window. This creates severe token inflation, increases quadratic self-attention latency, and induces hallucinations during arithmetic reasoning over heterogeneous observations. The paper OpenVLHarness: Real World Visual Agentic Tool-Use with Multimodal Memory (arXiv:2610.26860) details a concrete architectural solution that eliminates this bottleneck. articles.title: Text-to-Image Generative Modeling Without Language Pretraining
articles.summary: Modern text-to-image (T2I) systems use internet-scale language pretraining for text-conditioned image generation. We ask whether language pretraining is necessary for strong T2I generation. We introduce Halcyon, a family of early-fusion multimodal autoregressive models pretrained entirely from scratch on GPIC, a dataset of 100M image-text pairs. Halcyon-0.52B outperforms LlamaGen-XL/8 (48.0 vs. 63.3 gFD) with 18.2$\times$ less pretraining compute. Further, Halcyon-1.6B outperforms JiT-T2I-XXL/8++ (35.3 vs. 41.0 gFD) with 275$\times$ less pretraining compute. Controlled experiments show that text-only pretraining does not improve T2I generation. Halcyon also learns image captioning by replacing caption dropout with I2T supervision, maintaining competitive T2I generation quality under the same pretraining budget. We show that strong T2I systems can be trained from scratch without internet-scale language pretraining. Code and models are available at https://cs.stanford.edu/~keshik/halcyon

articles.title: Ropedia W0: Scaling Loco-Manipulation World Models across Embodiments with Human Experience
articles.summary: World models enable embodied agents to anticipate action consequences, yet jointly modeling locomotion and manipulation across diverse embodiments remains challenging due to heterogeneous action spaces and limited multimodal supervision. We present Ropedia W0, the first egocentric loco-manipulation world foundation model spanning humans and robots with diverse embodiments. We curate Xp-Data, comprising 10k hours of egocentric human data and 3k hours of robot data with unified multimodal annotations and systematic quality control. A unified kinematic representation encodes locomotion through camera poses and manipulation through projected skeletons, with robot skeletons combining embodiment-specific forward kinematics with extensive manual keypoint annotation and correction. We also introduce Xp-Teleop, a long-horizon loco-manipulation benchmark based on high-quality dexterous humanoid teleoperation data. articles.title: PlanarCityLoc: Breaking Silhouette Ambiguity in LoD Aerial Localization via 3D Planes
articles.summary: Aerial visual localization is crucial for autonomous drone navigation in urban environments where GNSS signals are often degraded. Lightweight textureless Level-of-Detail (LoD) city models provide a geometric map alternative to textured assets. Existing silhouette-based methods rely on image-space alignment, which can leave different camera poses indistinguishable and favor incorrect poses when segmentation errors distort the building outlines. We present PlanarCityLoc, which moves beyond silhouette overlap by leveraging the planar geometry of building facades and roofs. Following geometry-aware initialization, we match image-side planar patches to LoD model planes and use the resulting 3D-to-2D correspondences to refine pose with Perspective-n-Point (PnP). The framework uses off-the-shelf geometry and segmentation models without dataset-specific training or fine-tuning. articles.title: A(5) = 5: four matrices finish the case t = 5
articles.summary: This is from MV2's open notebook on Kakeya-type problems (https://github.com/munimtechnologies/kakeya-small-fields). It continues the earlier posts on finite 2-groups whose involutions are all central: is such a group at most |Omega_1|^(e+1), where 2^e is its exponent? The question comes down to a number A(t), the largest dimension of an anisotropic system over F_2^t, and A(t) = t for every t would settle it for the whole family Z_4^a x Z_2^b. An earlier post proved A(4) = 4. This one proves A(5) = 5: a short linear-algebra argument at four elements rules out the last remaining case at t = 5, and as a consequence the answer is yes for one more pair, Z_4^11 x Z_2^5. Lemma and section numbers point to notes in the repository. The result also rests on 12 answers of a SAT solver saved without proof certificates (job m13), and on Theorem 3.5 of C. de Seguins Pazzis (arXiv 1405.1575), which we cite and have not re-proved. articles.title: How to Run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next FP4 Locally (It Needs Blackwell and 55 Env Vars)
articles.summary: NVIDIA's FP4 build of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next is 96 GiB on disk. The BF16 original is about 355 GB. NVIDIA says the accuracy cost of that shrink is 0.7 points on GPQA Diamond. If you want to run Qwen3.8 Flash Next locally, that sounds like the obvious download. It isn't, at least not yet. The first line of the model card tells you upstream vLLM can't load it. Blackwell is the only supported architecture, and the RTX PRO 6000 launch script exports 55 environment variables before it gets to vllm serve. This post covers what NVIDIA changed, how the size stacks up against GGUF, which benchmark numbers hold up, and the run commands for RTX PRO 6000 and DGX Spark. My sources are the NVIDIA model card, the Qwen card, Unsloth's and bartowski's GGUF pages, and the community speed thread. I haven't run this checkpoint myself, so every number here comes from those pages, linked inline. What NVIDIA actually changed The base model is Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, released on August 26, 2026 (Qwen blog).

articles.title: StopWatch: Goal Grounding for Object-goal Navigation
articles.summary: Pretrained VLMs bring rich world knowledge and semantic priors to object-goal navigation, and fine-tuning a VLM into a navigation policy has become a common recipe. Despite this progress, success rates remain low, and it is unclear which capability these fine-tuned policies lack. Our diagnosis identifies goal grounding as the dominant failure. These policies explore well, yet often fail to notice that the goal is already in view or to estimate how far away it is. To address this failure, we ground the goal explicitly. Explicit grounding substantially improves success and reaches state-of-the-art results on six benchmarks across three scene collections. We also correct annotation defects in these benchmarks, so that future methods are evaluated more faithfully. Our analysis on the clean benchmarks shows that, with ground-truth grounding, our policy nearly matches the expert that generated its demonstrations, leaving the headroom in perception rather than policy learning. articles.title: Black Forest Labs' open-weights image model FLUX 3 Image Klein runs on consumer GPUs with just 8 GB of VRAM
articles.summary: Black Forest Labs has released FLUX 3 Image Klein, a 5.6-billion-parameter open-weights image model that supports native 4K generation, pixel-precise editing, and generation with up to ten reference images. With 38 percent fewer parameters than its predecessor, it still outperforms proprietary competitors in internal tests and runs on GPUs with just 8 GB of VRAM.
